items.title: Long-term rehabilitation needs of survivors of conflict-related sexual violence in Kosovo: a scoping review of challenges and policy directions.
items.authors: Limani M, Istrefi R, Limani M, Uwizeye G.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: More than two decades after the 1998-1999 Kosovo conflict, survivors of conflict-related sexual violence (CRSV) continue to experience profound long-term consequences across physical health, mental health, psychosocial wellbeing, economic stability, and social stigma. Despite landmark policy advances, including the 2014 legal status recognition, rehabilitation responses remain fragmented, under-resourced, and heavily dependent on the non-governmental sector. This scoping review maps the existing evidence on the long-term rehabilitation needs of CRSV survivors in Kosovo and identifies system-level barriers impeding access to comprehensive rehabilitation.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A scoping review was conducted following the Arksey and O'Malley framework, with reporting guided by the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Systematic searches were conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, supplemented by a targeted grey literature search using systematic methods Godin et al. across institutional websites and Google Advanced Search. Records were screened against Population-Concept-Context(PCC) eligibility criteria. Data were charted using a standardized extraction form and synthesized thematically across five rehabilitation domains.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A total of 37 sources were included: 19 peer-reviewed studies and 18 grey literature documents, including research and policy documents, government reports, non-governmental organization (NGO) reports, UN reports, and program evaluations. Sources spanned 2000-2025. Thematic synthesis identified five domains of unmet rehabilitation need: mental health and psychosocial wellbeing, physical health, legal and rights-based access, economic rehabilitation, and community reintegration. Four cross-cutting structural barriers were identified: the gap between legal recognition and substantive rehabilitation entitlements; NGO-state service dependency; stigma as a structural barrier; and unaddressed intergenerational trauma. The findings further highlight delayed accountability for CRSV as a critical constraint on rehabilitation.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Kosovo's CRSV rehabilitation landscape is characterized by substantial policy progress alongside persistent implementation gaps. Comprehensive survivor-centered rehabilitation requires institutionalization of services within the national health and social welfare system, a rights-based approach that links recognition to substantive entitlements, community-level norm change, and expanded attention to long-term and intergenerational impacts of trauma. Findings offer transferable lessons for other post-conflict settings where CRSV survivors remain underserved.

items.title: A Pragmatic Study of Brief, Low-Effort Implementation Strategies to Increase Reporting of Evidence-Based Practice Use in a Community Mental Health Program Implementing Multiple EBPs.
items.authors: Wright SP, Jacobs L.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Scaling evidence-based practices (EBPs) to address youth behavioral health needs is a key public health goal. Community mental health settings face challenges in measuring and reporting EBPs used with model fidelity due to resource constraints and complex reporting requirements, particularly when individual providers deliver multiple, distinct EBPs. This practical implementation report describes the development and evaluation of three implementation strategies to support the reporting of EBPs in a community mental health outpatient program in the state of Washington.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Using a pragmatic pre-post study design, we measured clinician EBP use via progress notes and billing claims data. After baseline data collection, we deployed three brief, low-effort implementation strategies, including developing educational materials, conducting an educational visit, and auditing and providing feedback. We compared internally calculated EBP use rates in our program to publicly available data from a state-affiliated reporting and implementation partner, and we characterized attempts to use EBP elements by providers who were not yet eligible to officially report EBP use at the state level.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The overall program EBP use rate was 32.7% in the baseline phase, and 48.9% after the implementation strategies were deployed. Paired pre-post analyses of eligible providers showed significant individual increases in EBP reporting post-deployment. The program's contribution to county-wide EBP services increased from 11.8% to 27.1% (with no change in relative proportion of total county services). Analysis of provider behavior that included all providers in the program supported the view that providers replaced informal use of EBP with formal EBP when possible and not simply a "report more EBP" response pattern.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: This report highlighted the potential benefits of deploying brief, low-effort implementation strategies to improve implementation outcomes, including self-reported reach and provider behavior. Characterizing EBP use among diverse provider types has practical utility for implementation research and practice.

items.title: An Exploration of the Communication Experiences Between Nonverbal Patients and Healthcare Professionals in Saudi Intensive Care: Patients.
items.authors: Alodan HA, Sutt AL, Hill R, Cross JL.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) are often mechanically ventilated, rendering them nonverbal and limiting their ability to interact with healthcare professionals (HCPs). Therefore, negative emotions such as irritation, anxiety, and dissatisfaction may arise. In the healthcare system of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA), language and cultural differences exist between patients and HCPs, raising further communication challenges for nonverbal patients in ICU. Despite this, however, no previous studies have explored the communication experiences of nonverbal patients in Saudi ICUs.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: The aim of this study was to explore the lived communication experiences of previously nonverbal patients in Saudi ICUs.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This study employed interpretive phenomenology based on Gadamer's philosophy. Using purposive sampling, five previously nonverbal ICU patients from two hospitals in KSA were interviewed. Data were interpreted following a hermeneutic circle and thematic analysis.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Patients' experiences revealed two themes: individual experience versus ICU care and elements of effective communication. Sedation affected physical and cognitive abilities of patients and pain was the most important topic to communicate. Nonverbal communication commonly occurred through unaided strategies, with a desire to use mobile devices and communication boards. While some patients had satisfactory communication experiences, others reported feeling negative attitude from HCPs. Patients emphasised that the language barrier affected their communication with non-Saudi HCPs. Ineffective communication caused negative emotions, including frustration and anger, leading patients to stop attempting further interactions. However, supportive communication seemingly improved patients' mental health and led to a speedier recovery.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: The communication experience of nonverbal patients in ICU varies and is influenced by their health status and interaction with HCPs. Communication strategies, HCPs attitude and behaviour, and overcoming the language barrier between patients and non-Saudi HCPs could positively influence the communication process.

Ineffective communication caused negative emotions, including frustration and anger, leading patients to stop attempting further interactions. However, supportive communication seemingly improved patients' mental health and led to a speedier recovery.

The communication experience of nonverbal patients in ICU varies and is influenced by their health status and interaction with HCPs. Communication strategies, HCPs attitude and behaviour, and overcoming the language barrier between patients and non-Saudi HCPs could positively influence the communication process.

items.title: Policies and Social Support Systems Addressing Mental Health and Social Isolation Among Older Adults in France and the United States - A Cross-National Perspective.
items.authors: Kelekar U, Das Gupta D, Law J.

sections.text: We investigated institutional support and sociocultural dynamics in France and the United States (US) that address social isolation among aging populations, a major risk factor for mental health conditions. Using public documents and a comparative qualitative approach, we summarized existing supports and interventions targeting social engagement and isolation among older adults in each country. We also conducted semistructured interviews with two independently living older adults in France and the US (age=89 years, female) to explore their aging experiences. Our interviews identified six key themes around reducing social isolation among older adults: (1) family support and intergenerational connectedness; (2) healthcare access; (3) direct opportunities for social participation; (4) indirect supports enabling engagement such as housing, transportation, home help; (5) technology use and digital integration; and (6) emergent themes including chronic disease management, resilience, and redefining identity. Our findings emphasize that inclusive policies and services, particularly in mobility and transportation, alongside personal resilience and informal support systems, are critical for reducing social isolation among older adults.

items.title: "Who Will Take Care of Us When We Get Older Than This?": A Qualitative Study With Older-Adult Gay Men and Transgender Women in Chiang Mai, Thailand.
items.authors: Tepjan S, Newman PA, Akkakanjanasupar P, Meiklejohn F, Fongkaew K, Hounnaklang N.
items.journal: Sexuality research & social policy : journal of NSRC : SR & SP

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Despite facing challenges that are distinct from their cisgender and heterosexual counterparts, few studies have engaged the voices and experiences of older-adult gay men and transgender women in Thailand.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: In-depth, semi-structured online interviews were conducted in Thai/Northern dialect to explore the lived experiences and perspectives of older-adult gay men ( n  = 9) and transgender women ( n  = 9) in rural, semi-urban, and urban settings in Chiang Mai province. Transcripts were reviewed using reflexive thematic analysis, with feminist care theory as a sensitizing framework.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Economic and health/mental health disparities accrued over lifetime experiences of marginalization engender specific care needs and resilience among older-adult gay men and transgender women. Reliance on kinship networks, Thailand's traditional source of elder care, was often precluded due to tenuous family relationships due to ongoing stigma and discrimination. Resilience expressed through attention to physical well-being, a spiritual outlook, financial planning, and community involvement suggest pathways to enhance healthy aging and care.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Incongruence between lived experiences of older-adult gay men and transgender women, and normative discourses of aging and care in Thailand, illustrate the inability of the present social welfare and healthcare systems to meet their needs, warranting focal inclusion of older LGBT+ adults in policymaking, research, and advocacy.

sections.heading: Policy implications
sections.text: Resource allocation, capacity-building, and training enabling local LGBT + and other community-based organizations to contribute competent care, support for informal LGBT+ older adult networks, and disaggregated national data on LGBT+ adults, may support culturally-relevant and evidence-based local care strategies for older LGBT+ adults that build on Thailand's collectivist orientation and Buddhist cultural strengths.

items.title: Designing a culturally responsive digital mental health E-clinic for women and adolescent girls in Jordan: A qualitative study.
items.authors: Alyahya M, Shattnawi K, Al-Sheyab N, Khader Y, Al-Shhab H.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Psychological distress among women and adolescent girls is a public health concern in low- and middle-income settings, where social adversity, stigma, displacement, and health-system constraints can hinder recognition and care. In Jordan, little is known about how healthcare providers recognize and respond to psychological distress within maternal, reproductive, and adolescent health services, or how they perceive culturally responsive digital mental health support. This study explored providers' perspectives, barriers to recognition and response, and the potential role of a digital mental health e-clinic.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: An interpretivist qualitative design using focus group discussions and in-depth interviews was adopted. A semi-structured guide explored clinical recognition of distress, service constraints, referral pathways, training and role-related challenges, and requirements for digital support. Audio-recorded Arabic data were transcribed verbatim, anonymized, and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The dataset comprised eight focus group discussions and four in-depth interviews. Providers recognized psychological distress through clinical observation, interpersonal cues, and professional experience, particularly during perinatal care. However, limited mental health training, heavy workloads, unclear professional authority, uneven institutional capacity, and fragmented referral pathways constrained assessment, documentation, and action. Participants viewed structured screening as an adjunct to clinical judgement for identifying individuals who may require further assessment and referral, but not as a diagnostic tool. They support digital tools when embedded within functioning care pathways and accompanied by professional training, supportive supervision, clear escalation procedures, confidentiality safeguards, and access to services.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: A culturally responsive digital mental health e-clinic may strengthen recognition, documentation, triage, referral, and continuity of care when integrated with clinical judgement and existing services. Digital tools should complement, not replace, professional assessment or specialist care. Improving mental health care for women and adolescent girls requires coordinated clinical, educational, service-level, and structural responses that address individual needs and wider social conditions contributing to psychological distress.

items.title: Food Noise in Obesity: Current Evidence, Measurement, and Clinical Implications.
items.authors: Ortiz-Martínez Y.

sections.text: Food noise has emerged as a patient-derived term describing frequent, persistent, or intrusive food-related thoughts that may be unwanted, distressing, or disruptive. Although the expression has rapidly entered public discourse, particularly alongside reports of appetite changes during glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) treatment, its scientific boundaries remain unsettled. This narrative review summarizes current definitions, epidemiologic observations, measurement instruments, proposed mechanisms, differential diagnosis, and responses to obesity interventions. Two dedicated instruments have been published: the five-item Food Noise Questionnaire (FNQ) and the Ro Allison Indiana Dhurandhar Food Noise Inventory (RAID-FN). Both demonstrate promising initial psychometric properties, but neither has established diagnostic thresholds, minimal clinically important differences, predictive validity, or sufficient evidence of responsiveness to treatment. Consumer surveys and selected cross-sectional studies suggest that burdensome food-related cognition is common in some populations; however, representative prevalence estimates are unavailable. Randomized trials show that glucagon-like peptide-1-based therapies reduce appetite, cravings, food-cue reactivity, and energy intake, whereas direct evidence of reduced food noise is currently limited primarily to retrospective and cross-sectional observations. Food noise should therefore be regarded as an emerging clinical dimension rather than a diagnosis, biomarker, or validated treatment target. Prospective studies using validated instruments are required to determine whether it provides information beyond established constructs and whether its reduction independently predicts weight-management, mental-health, or quality-of-life outcomes.

items.title: Systemic barriers to cultural knowledge integration in mental health practice.
items.authors: Brown J, Lengyell M.

sections.heading: Objectives
sections.text: In this theoretically driven narrative review, we examine epistemic injustice-specifically the systemic marginalization of certain groups as knowers and the inadequacy of dominant interpretive frameworks for accurately understanding their experiences. We explore how these dynamics manifest within Western mental health training and practice with the aim of advancing the theoretical application of the framework and developing recommendations for practice and institutional reform.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We applied Miranda Fricker's epistemic injustice framework to peer-reviewed literature published in PsycINFO and PubMed from 2000 to 2025 with the following terms: "epistemic injustice," "testimonial injustice," "hermeneutical injustice," "cultural competency," "traditional healing," "mental health disparities," "Indigenous psychology," and "multicultural therapy." The review is theoretically driven rather than systematic; source selection was iterative and judgment-based, and was informed by ongoing critical reflexivity regarding the authors' positionality relative to the communities described. Approximately 88 sources are drawn upon. The guiding research question is: how does epistemic injustice theory illuminate the structural mechanisms that sustain mental health disparities across diverse communities?

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Epistemic injustice operates through three interconnected levels: the exclusion of non-Western epistemologies in mental health training, testimonial and hermeneutical injustice in clinical encounters, and institutional mechanisms-including insurance structures, credentialing requirements, and evidence standards-that reproduce and reinforce the first two. These patterns are structural rather than incidental.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: We offer recommendations for transforming training programs, expanding the evidence framework, reforming institutional policies, and developing collaborative practice models that respect diverse healing traditions while addressing the epistemic conditions that sustain mental health disparities.

items.title: Why do we not have successful deradicalisation programmes? Impact measuring struggles in European and North American programme interventions.
items.authors: Maiberg H.

sections.text: Interventions aimed at supporting tertiary prevention (deradicalisation, disengagement, rehabilitation, and reintegration) should be designed according to participants' needs and employ a multi-agency approach that brings together relevant stakeholders connected to the case including organisations and services from local government, state authorities, and the third sector. To provide an overview of successful interventions in extremism prevention-particularly tertiary prevention programmes-it is necessary to measure their impact. However, only approximately 50% of practitioners involved in tertiary prevention programmes assess participant progress using standardised tools or predefined criteria to evaluate impact of the intervention. Based on 12 semi-structured interviews with tertiary prevention programme providers from Europe and North America, this article analyses how "success" is defined by members of the sample. It also maps and categorises methods used in prevention interventions, including psychiatric care and trauma-informed approaches, and examines the role of practitioners' professional and/or academic backgrounds in the selection of intervention methods. The results show that understanding of key terminology, working methods and whether impact is measured in the sample group from Europe and North America vary amongst intervention providers, including those who have been former extremists. This article suggests that without standardised terminology, working methods and training principles for intervention providers, impact, including success of interventions cannot be measured. As named problems affect global communities equally, practitioners, policymakers, and researchers are encouraged to create results in the form of "soft law" where the key ways to measure necessary types of impact, suggested working methods to support tertiary prevention processes, including guidance on choosing working methods for a tailor-made approach, are agreed.

items.title: Dyadic coping and resilience in Chinese female patients with connective tissue disease and their spouses: an actor-partner interdependence model analysis.
items.authors: Cai X, Xu S, Zhong X, Dong C, Gu Z.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Connective tissue disease (CTD), being an incurable lifelong condition, is significantly correlated with patients' psychological well-being during prolonged treatment. This study aims to offer insights into improving mental health by examining the relationship between dyadic coping and psychological resilience in patients and their spouses.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A cross-sectional study was conducted in the Department of Rheumatology and Immunology at the Affiliated Hospital of Nantong University between October 2023 and October 2024. Guided by the Actor-Partner Interdependence Model, this study analyzed the relationship between dyadic coping and psychological resilience in female patients and their spouses.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A total of 231 couples were included in the study, and 68.40% of female respondents were less than 35 years old; 70.56% of couples lived in urban. About 93.07% of females and 96.54% of males were employed; 16.88% of females did not know about CTD, and 15.15% of their spouses did not know about CTD. The average scores in resilience of patients and spouses were 64.913 (SD = 16.592) and 64.970 (SD = 19.973); The positive dyadic coping scores of the patients and their spouses were 102.351 ± 20.737 and 101.476 ± 21.854, the scores of negative dyadic coping were 20.108 ± 10.566 and 20.416 ± 10.431. In the path analysis of APIM, patients' higher dyadic coping was associated with their own greater resilience, yet patients' higher dyadic coping correlated with spouses' lower resilience in Model 1, and positive dyadic coping was positively associated with one's own resilience (actor effect), but the spouse-to-patient partner path was not significant in Model 2. Furthermore, the partner effect between patients' positive dyadic coping and spouses' resilience was positively associated. The path analysis of the actor effect and partner effect between negative dyadic coping and resilience showed that couples' dyadic coping negatively correlated with resilience.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The findings indicated that dyadic coping levels were significantly associated with psychological resilience, particularly negative dyadic coping. Connective tissue diseases require long-term management, and positive dyadic coping was positively associated with patients' own resilience (actor effect), whereas the partner effect of spouses' positive dyadic coping on patients' resilience was not significant.

items.title: Reimagining postpartum care to advance health equity: A qualitative study with Black postpartum individuals and health workers.
items.authors: Arrington LA, Jeffers NK, Bradford HM, Snowden E, Whitfield OA, Eden P, Marcelle E, Marea CX.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Our qualitative study aimed to determine the critical components of postpartum care for Black individuals in order to design and implement a reimagined postpartum care model that promotes health and wellness for families experiencing racism in Washington, D.C. (DC).

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We partnered with Community of Hope, a DC community-based organization, to conduct focus group discussions with Black postpartum individuals and health workers. We used the 5D Cycle for Health Equity to explore Black postpartum individuals' and health workers' definitions and measures of harm and health equity (ReDefine), practices to achieve wellness (Discover), and dreams for equitable and anti-oppressive care (Dream) during the postpartum period.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: We conducted eight focus groups - four with Black postpartum individuals (n=23) and four with health workers (n=19). Participants critiqued the 6-week limit to care and lack of time and resources for comprehensive postpartum support. They recalled circumventing inadequate care by seeking material and community support. They dreamed of a holistic, accessible, and attentive care team to address physical and mental health, social support, and material postpartum needs.

sections.heading: Discussion and conclusion
sections.text: We applied the 5D Cycle for Health Equity to a community-engaged participatory research methodology and determined the critical components of postpartum care from the perspective of Black postpartum individuals and health workers.

sections.heading: Health equity implications
sections.text: By centering the needs, experiences, and expertise of an oppressed group, these study findings suggest reimagining comprehensive care models to enhance quality, holistically address complex postpartum needs, and lay a foundation for just care for all.

items.title: New-onset depersonalization-derealization syndrome following semaglutide therapy.
items.authors: Prasad S, Sharma A, Sharma A, Parmar V, Kothia D, Bavaria D.

sections.text: Semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist prescribed for type 2 diabetes and obesity, acts on central neuropsychiatric pathways beyond its metabolic effects, yet dissociative adverse effects have rarely been reported. We describe a 42-year-old woman with no psychiatric history who developed recurrent, distressing episodes of depersonalization and derealization approximately 7 days after her second 0.5 mg weekly dose of semaglutide prescribed for obesity. The episodes progressed from once daily to 3 to 4 times daily over 10 days, with insight and reality testing preserved throughout. Metabolic, neurological, toxicological, and psychiatric evaluations, including brain imaging, electroencephalography, and laboratory studies, excluded alternative causes. She fulfilled the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition criteria for depersonalization-derealization disorder, and the Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale score of 6 indicated a probable causal relationship. Semaglutide was discontinued without psychotropic medication, and symptoms resolved completely within 4 weeks, with sustained remission at 3 months. This case suggests that depersonalization-derealization is an underrecognized, reversible neuropsychiatric adverse effect of semaglutide and underscores the need for clinician awareness and patient counseling during therapy.

items.title: Efficacy and Safety of Supramolecular Salicylic Acid Combined With Intense Pulsed Light for Rosacea: A Split-Face Trial.
items.authors: Wang M, Tan A, Zhuo F.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder with a global prevalence of approximately 5.46%, significantly impairing patients' quality of life and mental health. We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of supramolecular salicylic acid (SSA) peeling combined with intense pulsed light (IPL) for rosacea and its impact on skin barrier function.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Thirty-six patients with erythematotelangiectatic or papulopustular rosacea were enrolled in this split-face study. All patients received full-face IPL treatment monthly for three sessions; a randomly assigned facial half underwent a 30% SSA peel per session. Efficacy was assessed using the VISIA Complexion Analysis System and the CK multiple probe adapter. The Clinical Erythema Assessment (CEA) and patient self-assessment served as secondary outcomes. Skin hydration and transepidermal water loss (TEWL) were monitored to evaluate the skin barrier.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Thirty-three patients completed the trial (three dropouts). After 3 months, the combination side showed significantly greater reductions in VISIA erythema scores (-3.32 ± 3.81 vs. -1.88 ± 2.58; p  = 0.0041) and CK erythema index (-36.09 ± 20.80 vs. -25.88 ± 25.86; p  = 0.0013) than the IPL-alone side. Both sides showed significant improvement in CEA and patient self-assessment ( p  < 0.05), with no statistically significant inter-side difference. Skin hydration increased while TEWL decreased bilaterally ( p  < 0.05). Adverse events were mild and comparable between sides ( p  = 0.476).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: SSA peeling combined with IPL is superior to IPL monotherapy for rosacea erythema, offering enhanced efficacy without compromising skin barrier function.

items.title: Exploring the Links Between Body Dysmorphic Concerns and Acceptance of Cosmetic Surgery: The Role of Internal and External Shame as Mediators.
items.authors: Topalian GV, Al Tekle GA, Iskandar K, Lahoud P, Fekih-Romdhane F, Hallit S, Obeid S.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Cosmetic surgery has become increasingly normalized in many societies, including Lebanon, where appearance enhancement is often associated with identity, social acceptance, and social mobility. Body dysmorphic concerns (BDC) and shame have both been associated with attitudes toward cosmetic surgery; however, the emotional processes underlying these associations remain insufficiently explored. The purpose of this study is to assess the mediating role of shame in the relationship between BDC and acceptance of cosmetic surgery in Lebanese adults.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: In this cross-sectional study, 399 Lebanese participants aged 18 years and older were enrolled. Measures used were the Acceptance of Cosmetic Surgery Scale (ACSS), the Dysmorphic Concern Questionnaire (DCQ), a screening measure of subclinical dysmorphic concerns, and the External and Internal Shame Scale (EISS).

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Indirect associations statistically consistent with partial mediation models involving total, internal, and external shame were observed between BDC and acceptance of cosmetic surgery. Higher BDC was significantly associated with higher shame and directly associated with higher acceptance of cosmetic surgery. Higher shame was significantly associated with lower acceptance of cosmetic surgery.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: These results indicate that the role of shame in crafting attitudes toward cosmetic surgery is rather complicated as an emotional variable. BDC and shame can be screened for during preoperative consultations by clinicians to determine which patients are at risk of having psychological concerns. Applying mental health care to the perspective of aesthetic medicine can increase patient satisfaction and result in an ethical, patient-centered approach.

items.title: Proof of concept using vocational tele-cognitive rehabilitation to improve work status in primary brain tumor.
items.authors: Weyer Jamora C, Brie MS, Bracci PM, Smith EM, Luks TL, Phan S, Braunstein SE, Oberheim-Bush NA, Butowski NA, Clarke JL, De Groot J, Chang SM, Nelson MD, Hervey-Jumper SL, Taylor JW.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Survivors of primary brain tumors (SPBT) frequently struggle to return to work. This study investigated work status and outcomes after tele-based vocational cognitive rehabilitation (t-VCR) in SPBT.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We retrospectively reviewed adults (≤65 years) with SPBT at an academic medical center who completed objective cognitive and patient-reported outcome measures between 5/2018 and 5/2022. Participants were grouped by employment status and compared on demographic and clinical characteristics. Work outcomes were analyzed in a subgroup who underwent t-VCR during standard clinical care. t-VCR treatment response was defined as return to work, increase to full-time work, or graduation from a workplace improvement plan versus baseline. Analyses used t-tests, chi-square, and McNemar tests, with content analysis identifying key interventions in responders.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Of 77 participants, 35 were working and 42 were unemployed upon referral. Unemployment was associated with worsened verbal learning and memory ( P  < .003). Among the 28 people who received t-VCR (mean-10 sessions), 82% returned to work after t-VCR. In those who had improved work status, content analysis identified t-VCR interventions, including executive and organizational skills training, mental health counseling, job simulations/accommodations, and fatigue/stimulation education were most common.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Worsened verbal learning and memory were associated with unemployment, highlighting the impact these cognitive symptoms can have on occupational functioning. Work status improved in the context of t-VCR and warrants further study. Among participants who demonstrated improvement, t-VCR was delivered as a multimodal, individualized intervention that addressed cognitive, emotional, fatigue, and practical workplace-related challenges.

items.title: Relationship between the provision of procedures in psychosocial care centers and socioeconomic factors: an ecological study.
items.authors: Lima AHS, Coelho AA, Costa GMC, Olinda RA, Silva VCD.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: to analyze the correlation between the supply of procedures performed in the Psychosocial Care Centers and the socioeconomic indicators in municipalities with populations above 100 thousand inhabitants.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: this is an ecological study covering 312 municipalities and 1,127 services. In the modeling, data were extracted from the historical series of outpatient production of the Health Information System and socioeconomic indicators from the Atlas of Human Development.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: only 12 capitals recorded harm reduction actions; 93% of the records are more frequent in the capitals. A positive correlation was observed between home care and per capita income; and a negative correlation between psychosocial rehabilitation and illiteracy rate. It is noteworthy that the Municipal Human Development Index and per capita income were correlated with most of the procedures, while the illiteracy rate correlated with 64.7% of them. Statistically significant differences were found between medium and large municipalities.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: the relationship between the procedures recorded in the Psychosocial Care Centers and the socioeconomic indicators may indicate the influence of multifactorial issues on mental health care.

items.title: Evolutionary selection pressures give rise to risky preferences in value-based decision-making.
items.authors: Wu J, Pulcu E.

sections.text: We are living in a dynamically changing world, where optimal decision-making under uncertainty is linked to the survival of species. However, evolutionary selection pressures that shape value-based decision-making (VBDM, i.e. choosing between available options based on their expected value) under uncertainty have received only limited attention. The current work demonstrates that fitness associated with different VBDM preferences is influenced by the value properties of the environment, as well as the characteristics and the density of competitors in the population. Computational model-based analysis shows that, when there are an increasingly large number of discrete strategies competing for fitness, risk-seeking tendencies can eventually dominate the population. We demonstrate that the strength of these strategies was minimizing suboptimal decisions by tracking the expected value difference between available options more precisely. We discuss the broad implications of our finding across behavioural ecology, behavioural economics and also in relation to the evolutionary basis of vulnerability to psychiatric conditions such as gambling addiction.

items.title: Medication knowledge in psychiatric day hospital patients: The role of polypharmacy.
items.authors: Queck LS, Heck J, Krause O, Klietz M, Kümpers F, Vagi RK, Groh A, Schulze Westhoff M, Schröder S.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Adequate medication knowledge of patients is critical for medication safety, particularly among psychiatric patients exposed to complex pharmacotherapy. However, data on patients treated in psychiatric day hospital settings are limited.

sections.heading: Objectives
sections.text: This study aimed to assess medication knowledge and identify factors associated with knowledge gaps in this population.

sections.heading: Design
sections.text: Cross-sectional observational study.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A total of 101 patients from a psychiatric day hospital were included. Medication knowledge was assessed using a structured interviewer-administered questionnaire covering drug name, indication, dosage and administration schedule (possible score range: 0-6). Group differences and associations were analysed using Mann-Whitney U tests, Kruskal-Wallis tests and Spearman correlations.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The median medication knowledge score was 4.3 (interquartile range (IQR) 3.0-5.8). A moderate negative correlation was observed between the number of medications taken and knowledge (ρ = -0.404, p < 0.001). Knowledge was not associated with sex (p = 0.29) or age (ρ = -0.093, p = 0.353). Knowledge differed significantly across drug classes (p < 0.001), being highest for nervous system drugs. Discrepancies between prescribed and reported medication were frequent, with 29 patients reporting 44 additional undocumented medications. The internet (31.7%) and medical specialists (30.7%) were the most reported sources of medication-related information.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Medication knowledge among psychiatric day hospital patients varied considerably and was lower among patients receiving a higher number of medications. Frequent discrepancies between documented and patient-reported medication use were observed, indicating a potential risk for unsafe medication use. In addition, insufficient medication knowledge may represent a clinically relevant risk factor for medication-related problems. Targeted, patient-centred education strategies should be prioritized to improve medication safety in this setting.
